# Material and Methods

The methodology of this thesis is structured around two primary phases. The first phase establishes the underlying ecological algorithm, detailing the data processing and statistical pipeline required to generate a wild boar resistance surface. The second phase focuses on translating this workflow into an applied software solution through the development of an automated, user-facing QGIS plugin. Together, these sections outline both the ecological logic required to model habitat connectivity and the software engineering steps used to package this pipeline into a functional tool.

## Software Environment and Data Inputs

This section details the computational tools and empirical datasets required to construct the resistance surface pipeline and develop the automated QGIS tool. It outlines the programming frameworks used for geoprocessing, as well as the specific biological and spatial datasets necessary to calibrate and validate the underlying ecological model.

### Development Environment

The development of the resistance surface pipeline and the subsequent QGIS plugin required a dual-language software environment, combining R and Python.

The ecological algorithm, encompassing the step-selection analysis and initial model calibration, was developed in R (version 4.5.1). Spatial data handling and vector operations were executed using the `terra` (version 1.9.11) and `sf` (version 1.1.0) packages, while movement ecology metrics and track resampling were processed with `amt` (version 0.3.1.0). Data wrangling and temporal operations were performed using `dplyr` (version 1.2.1), `tidyr` (version 1.3.1), `purrr` (version 1.1.0), and `lubridate` (version 1.9.4). The integrated step-selection function was fitted via conditional logistic regression using the `survival` package (version 3.8.3), with model outputs standardized using `broom` (version 1.0.10). Statistical visualizations were produced with `ggplot2` (version 4.0.3). Multicollinearity diagnostics were computed using the `car` package via the variance inflation factor procedure described in the variable selection section below.

The automated tool was implemented as a QGIS plugin (version 3.40.13) named *Wildboar Connectivity (ASF)*, version 0.4. The plugin's backend geoprocessing logic and graphical user interface were written in Python (version 3.11.5).

### Calibration and Testing Data

To delineate the spatial extent of the study, administrative boundaries were extracted from the `tlm_kantonsgebiet` layer of the swissBOUNDARIES3D dataset. Canton Aargau served as the primary training area to calibrate the ecological resistance model, while Canton Zürich was designated as the independent transfer area to evaluate the automated QGIS tool. To mitigate spatial edge effects during the geoprocessing phases, a geometric buffer of 2,000 metres was applied around each cantonal perimeter, and the resulting geometry was converted into a rectangular bounding box using the `st_as_sfc` function. Because the high-resolution environmental covariates used in this project are restricted to Swiss national territory, this rectangular extent was subsequently intersected with the national boundary so that it does not extend into Germany.

While Canton Aargau shares a direct northern border with Germany, extending the study area across the border was explicitly excluded from the experimental design. Combining Swiss topographical and land cover data with corresponding German datasets would have required complex harmonization of disparate semantic classifications, such as reconciling swissTLM3D object types with German ATKIS categories, as well as differences in native spatial resolutions and coordinate reference systems. Replacing national datasets with pan-European alternatives such as CORINE Land Cover was also considered and rejected, because transnational datasets typically operate at resolutions of 100 metres or coarser and use generalized land cover classifications that fail to capture narrow forest corridors, minor roads, and other micro-habitat structures that are decisive for wild boar movement at the scale of a 15-minute GPS fix interval. The study area was therefore restricted strictly to Swiss territory, accepting a marginal edge effect at the northern border in exchange for the full resolution and thematic depth of national geodatasets.

To ensure strict spatial alignment across all pipeline outputs, a master raster grid was generated for each canton. This grid was standardized to the Swiss coordinate reference system LV95 (EPSG:2056) at a uniform spatial resolution of 25 metres. To optimize computational efficiency during the loading and masking of large environmental covariate datasets, the geometry of each buffered study area was converted into a Well-Known Text (WKT) string and passed directly as a spatial filter into the vector reading functions of the `sf` package. This approach substantially reduces memory load by loading only the geometries that intersect the relevant extent rather than reading entire nationwide geodatabases.

### Wild Boar Telemetry Data

The biological foundation of the model consisted of a GPS telemetry dataset of wild boars (*Sus scrofa*) collected by the Wildlife Management Research Group (WILMA, ZHAW) as part of the Wildschweinschreck project. Between 2014 and 2017, a total of 36 individuals were equipped with GSM-GPS tracking collars (VECTRONIC Aerospace) within the Aargau study areas of Elfingen and Felsenau. The devices were programmed to record a spatial location at a standard interval of 15 minutes.

The primary methodological benefit of integrating this dataset was that it enabled a strictly empirical approach to constructing the resistance surface. Rather than defining landscape permeability based on expert opinion, the high-frequency GPS data allowed for the estimation of a data-driven Step-Selection Function. This approach ensures that the final resistance values objectively reflect the quantifiable movement behaviour of the animals, providing a robust biological foundation for the tool.

The raw dataset exhibited considerable heterogeneity. It contained numerous secondary attributes, such as sun and moon phase annotations and distances to forest edges, which were not retained in the current pipeline. A notable limitation was the incomplete temporal coverage of some attributes in the data, for example the agricultural crop attribute ("Frucht" column), which was only recorded systematically during specific field surveys in the summer months and was therefore excluded entirely. Temporal intervals between GPS points showed irregularities caused by signal loss and collar disconnections. The detailed preprocessing steps undertaken to regularize these timestamps and clean the dataset are described in the subsequent section on telemetry processing.

### SwissBOUNDARIES3D

To delineate the precise spatial extent of the study areas, the swissBOUNDARIES3D dataset (version 1.5) was used. Provided by the Federal Office of Topography (swisstopo), this vector dataset contains the administrative boundaries of Switzerland in three-dimensional format, with geometries defined as sequences of three-dimensional coordinates derived by projecting administrative borders onto the digital elevation model swissALTI3D. The dataset was implemented in GeoPackage format, standardized to the Swiss coordinate reference system LV95 (LN02).

The primary benefit of swissBOUNDARIES3D lies in its role as a foundational reference dataset designed for exact integration with other national geodatasets. It features homogeneous nationwide quality with a geometric accuracy of $\pm0.5$ metres in both position and elevation, continuously verified through original cadastral surveying data. Within the geoprocessing pipeline, the polygon feature class `TLM_KANTONSGEBIET` was targeted to extract the administrative geometries of Canton Aargau and Canton Zürich.

Despite its technical precision, relying on this dataset introduces an inherent ecological limitation: administrative boundaries are political constructs that rarely align with natural topography or continuous wildlife habitats. To prevent abrupt boundary cut-offs from introducing artificial edge effects into the resistance model, the extracted geometries were buffered by 2,000 metres and converted into a rectangular processing extent rather than used as hard spatial limits.

### SwissTLM3D

To represent the spatial configuration of land cover and anthropogenic infrastructure, the Topographic Landscape Model swissTLM3D (2026 edition), provided by swisstopo, was incorporated as the primary source for environmental covariates. The dataset was used in GeoPackage format, standardized to the LV95 coordinate reference system.

The primary benefit of swissTLM3D was its thematic depth and high spatial accuracy, which allowed for the targeted extraction of landscape elements known to govern wild boar movement and habitat selection. To model protective cover and primary habitat, natural vegetation classes were extracted from the `tlm_bb_bodenbedeckung` layer based on the `objektart` attribute, retaining closed forest ("Wald"), open forest ("Wald offen"), scrub ("Gebueschwald"), and woody areas ("Gehoelzflaeche"). Land-use types that act as barriers or fail to provide consistent cover were excluded from the available habitat matrix, specifically: unstocked forests ("Wald nicht bestockt"), mining areas ("Abbauareal"), orchards ("Obstanlage"), cemeteries ("Friedhof"), vineyards ("Reben"), and water body areas ("Gewaesserareal").

The road network was classified into three ecologically meaningful categories from the `tlm_strassen_strasse` layer. Fenced high-performance roads — "Autobahn", "Autostrasse", "Ausfahrt", "Einfahrt", "Zufahrt", and "Autozug" — represent infrastructure that is comprehensively fenced under federal regulation and physically impassable to wild boar under normal conditions. Main roads — "10m Strasse", "8m Strasse", and "6m Strasse" — correspond to primary through-roads that elicit strong avoidance but remain physically crossable. Secondary roads — "4m Strasse", "3m Strasse", "Verbindung", and "Dienstzufahrt" — cover narrower drivable roads, agricultural service roads, and forest tracks. Settlement boundaries were mapped using the `tlm_namen_siedlungsname` polygon layer, retaining the four granularity classes "Ort", "Ortsteil", "Quartier", and "Quartierteil" to ensure complete coverage of the built-up matrix. The settlement polygon approach was preferred over individual building footprints because wild boar respond to the contiguous built-up matrix characterized by noise, light, and human activity rather than to the geometry of individual structures.

A key preprocessing feature of swissTLM3D relevant to this study was the `KUNSTBAUTE` attribute, which encodes engineered structures on linear features. Combined with the numeric vertical-position attribute `STUFE`, this allowed the pipeline to identify and remove all infrastructure segments located below ground level, such as tunnels, underpasses, and roads inside buildings, before computing distance rasters. The rationale and implementation of this filtering step are described in detail in the spatial covariates section.

Despite its cartographic quality, swissTLM3D represents a static snapshot of the landscape. It cannot account for seasonal variations relevant to wild boar ecology, such as the shifting presence of maize crops or temporary human disturbance, and its land cover classifications are designed for topographic mapping rather than biological modeling, meaning that a polygon classified as "Wald" does not quantify understory density.

### DHM25

To establish the topographic foundation of the resistance surface, the Digital Height Model DHM25 (`dhm25_grid_raster.asc`) was incorporated into the spatial pipeline. Sourced from swisstopo, this model represents the three-dimensional shape of the earth's surface, excluding vegetation and built structures, at a uniform spatial resolution of 25 metres. The dataset was used in its native ASCII grid format and is originally referenced to the Swiss LV03 coordinate system (EPSG:21781).

The primary benefit of the DHM25 for this project was its direct alignment with the target spatial scale of the resistance surface. Because the master grid was designed at 25-metre resolution, the DHM25 provided a perfectly matched topographic baseline from which slope and the Terrain Ruggedness Index could be derived without resampling. Using this pre-rasterized 25-metre model avoided the severe computational overhead of aggregating modern high-resolution LiDAR datasets across multiple cantonal extents.

The DHM25 is built on a historical foundation, having been derived from digitized contour lines and spot heights of the official Swiss National Map 1:25,000. Its vertical accuracy is $\pm1.5$ metres on average for the Swiss Plateau and $\pm3$ to $\pm8$ metres in Alpine and Pre-Alpine terrain. However, the DHM25 is a legacy dataset whose fundamental altitude data was primarily surveyed between 1952 and 1979, with final updates concluded in 1999. Significant recent terrain alterations such as highway earthworks or large-scale quarry expansions are therefore not reflected in the topography. Because it is strictly a bare-earth terrain model, it also contains no information about forest canopy height or density, making it necessary to combine topographic covariates with the land cover data from swissTLM3D to adequately model forest structure.

### Wildlife Passages

To model points of localized permeability across major anthropogenic barriers, the national geodatabase of wildlife passages (`Wildtierpassagen.gdb`), issued by the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN), was integrated. The specific polygon layer `N2023_Version_Wildtierpassagen`, representing the 2023 update in the LV95 coordinate reference system, was used.

The functional role of this dataset was to override the absolute barrier effect of fenced motorways at verified crossing structures. In a baseline resistance raster, a fenced motorway is represented as a continuous impassable line. By rasterizing wildlife passage polygons onto this surface after all other burn-in operations, these specific locations could be assigned minimum resistance values, ensuring that connectivity pathways realistically reflect the movement opportunities available to wild boar rather than treating motorways as uniformly impenetrable. Geometries were buffered by 30 metres before rasterization to ensure that the full crossing structure, including approach ramps and adjacent fenced corridors, was captured at the 25-metre raster resolution.

A notable limitation of this dataset is its restriction to dedicated wildlife crossing structures such as green bridges and specialized underpasses. It does not map multi-use infrastructure that wild boar frequently exploit, such as agricultural underpasses or large drainage culverts. The resistance surface therefore likely underestimates the true fine-scale permeability of the landscape at locations where undocumented crossing structures exist.

### Permanent Fences Canton Zürich

To incorporate verified anthropogenic barriers into the Zürich transfer area, a vector dataset of permanent woven-wire fences (`Dauerzaeune.shp`) was used. Sourced from the Cantonal Veterinary Office of Zürich, this shapefile delineates fencing structures constructed as preventive barriers against the spread of African Swine Fever. The polygon geometries represent the exact spatial extent of these installations.

Within the resistance model, these fences were treated as absolute barriers, assigned `NA` values in the final Zürich resistance raster. Unlike typical agricultural fencing, which most ungulates can jump, ASF protection fences are explicitly engineered to be wild-boar-proof, making this maximum resistance assignment biologically appropriate. The dataset covers major, officially documented installations and does not capture temporary agricultural fencing or small-scale private enclosures, which means that certain fine-scale barriers influencing movement in the real landscape are not reflected in the final surface.

### Wild Boar Habitats Canton of Zürich

To provide spatial validation anchors for the tool's transfer to the independent study area, the shapefile `Potenzial_Wildschwein_Kerneinstaende_ZH_2024_WILMA.shp` was incorporated. Developed in December 2024 by WILMA (ZHAW), commissioned by the Cantonal Veterinary Office of Zürich, this dataset spatially delineates potential core resting habitats for wild boar across the canton, capturing landscape structures required for daytime refuge and shelter.

Because the GPS telemetry used to calibrate the resistance model was strictly limited to Canton Aargau, this shapefile provided the biological reference points needed to evaluate whether the pipeline, parameterized entirely on Aargau data, could identify functionally meaningful connectivity corridors between ecologically suitable patches in a novel landscape. The dataset is predictive in nature, derived from spatial parameters and expert criteria rather than empirical GPS tracking from wild boar currently resident in Zürich. It was therefore used to assess the spatial plausibility of the modeled corridors rather than to confirm the physical presence of animals at specific locations.

## Resistance Surface Pipeline

This section describes the analytical framework used to convert empirical animal movement data into a spatially continuous resistance surface at 25-metre resolution. The pipeline was structured around three sequential phases: the regularization and behavioral classification of raw GPS telemetry, the empirical estimation of habitat preferences via an integrated step-selection function, and the mathematical transformation of the resulting statistical coefficients into landscape resistance values via the Keeley exponential transformation. The methodological design was adapted from the connectivity frameworks of @fischer2024, @clontz2021, and @keeley2016. All calibration and validation steps were prototyped and executed in the R programming environment to ensure the statistical robustness and ecological validity of the baseline model before the algorithm was translated into the Python architecture of the QGIS plugin.

### Telemetry Processing

All telemetry processing was conducted in R with all spatial geometries standardized to LV95 (EPSG:2056). The raw GPS dataset was subjected to a systematic cleaning protocol before any movement calculations were performed. All timestamps were parsed and standardized to UTC. Spatial validity checks removed records with missing or implausible coordinates by enforcing plausibility bounds consistent with Swiss national coordinate ranges. To eliminate behavioral anomalies associated with the collaring procedure, the first five days of tracking data for each individual were dropped as a capture-shock buffer. Any individual deployment containing fewer than 100 GPS fixes or spanning less than 30 days after this initial cleaning was excluded from all subsequent analysis to ensure statistical robustness. One specific deployment, `027_Agat_13970`, was excluded from the analysis because it represented a short re-collaring of an animal already well represented by a separate, longer deployment (`027_Agat_13969`), and its fix quality was substantially lower, with only 50.6 percent of scheduled fixes recorded on time and elevated proportions of short and medium temporal gaps.

Following the initial cleaning, the continuous tracking data were converted into discrete movement steps using the `amt` package. Trajectories were resampled to a consistent 15-minute interval with a tolerance of five minutes using `track_resample()`, which retains at most one fix per 20-minute window and thereby collapses redundant secondary fixes recorded at sub-15-minute intervals in some deployments. Because the raw data contained irregular interruptions and missing fixes, the resampled trajectories were processed using `steps_by_burst()`, which automatically segments each track into temporally continuous runs and calculates step lengths and turning angles exclusively within those runs. Any gap exceeding the 20-minute maximum threshold terminates the current burst, preventing the algorithm from constructing a spurious step length across a data gap. For certain individuals such as `027_Agat_13969` and `039_Pete_12272`, the resampling retained approximately 60 to 70 percent of raw fixes. This represents expected deduplication of redundant secondary fixes rather than biological data loss.

### Step Classification

Because a resistance surface models the energetic cost of traveling between habitat patches rather than foraging or resting within them, it was necessary to separate the telemetry into two behavioral states: in-patch steps, representing stationary or localized behavior, and in-matrix steps, representing directed transit between patches.

The baseline approach used for red deer connectivity modeling by @fischer2024 relied on fractal analysis combined with k-means clustering and a Gaussian Mixture Model to classify step behavior. Initial testing showed this approach to be biologically inappropriate for wild boar. Red deer exhibit clearly distinct spatial separation between stationary behavior and large-scale seasonal migration. Wild boar are highly resident animals that generally remain within a defined home range and only undertake long, directed movements in response to social dispersal, severe disturbance, or drastic landscape change. The two behavioral modes are therefore far less spatially separated in wild boar telemetry than in red deer, and a density-based mixture model cannot reliably distinguish them in this species.

A rule-based classifier was therefore developed to identify directed transit steps by their geometric properties. The classifier evaluates each step in order using the following three rules, applied within each individual burst so that temporal gaps in the GPS schedule do not chain steps from different time periods.

1. A step length strictly greater than 250 metres is classified as in-matrix, reflecting long-distance directed transit [@podgorski2013].
2. A step length greater than 150 metres combined with a turning angle of less than $\pi/4$ radians in absolute value is classified as in-matrix, indicating medium-distance directional movement [@clontz2021].
3. Three or more consecutive steps within the same burst all exceeding 100 metres in length and all exhibiting a turning angle below $\pi/4$ radians in absolute value are classified as in-matrix as a group, capturing sustained directional travel over a 45-minute period and reducing false positives from isolated long steps caused by GPS noise [@benhamou2014].

All steps that did not satisfy any of these conditions were classified as in-patch. Only the in-matrix steps were retained for the subsequent iSSF fitting.

### Spatial Covariates

Following behavioral classification, the environmental covariates required for the iSSF were derived and aligned to the 25-metre LV95 master grid. Each layer was processed using the buffered cantonal extent as its spatial domain, ensuring that focal statistics and distance calculations near the canton boundary were not biased by edge effects from the abrupt study area limit.

#### Forest Cover and Structure

Forest availability and structure were derived from the `tlm_bb_bodenbedeckung` layer within swissTLM3D. Three complementary forest layers were constructed to capture different spatial scales of forest influence on wild boar movement.

A binary forest mask was created by filtering polygons to the four forest object types and rasterizing them onto the master grid with `touches = TRUE`. The all-touched inclusion rule ensures that any 25-metre pixel intersected by a forest polygon, regardless of the fraction of overlap, is classified as forest. This choice was essential for preserving narrow tree lines, hedgerows, and small copses, which frequently function as movement corridors and stepping-stone habitats in predominantly agricultural landscapes.

Local forest density at the 50-metre scale was calculated by applying a circular focal window with a 50-metre radius to the binary forest raster. The focal weights were converted into a Boolean mask prior to computation, so that the resulting value at each pixel represents the exact proportion of forested pixels within the surrounding disk, ranging from 0.0 to 1.0. This covariate captures the structural density of the immediate habitat context, distinguishing sparse fragmented cover from continuous woodland.

Forest density at the 1000-metre scale was calculated using the same approach with a 1000-metre radius focal window. This macro-scale covariate captures the broader forest complex that provides population-level habitat and long-range landscape context for movement decisions. Including both the 50-metre and 1000-metre density variables in the model allowed the iSSF to estimate separate selection coefficients for immediate micro-canopy security and macro-level forest patch size, representing the two spatial orders of habitat selection described by @johnson1980.

An unsigned distance-to-forest-edge covariate was also computed. For pixels located in open terrain, the Euclidean distance to the nearest forested pixel was calculated. For pixels located inside forest, the Euclidean distance to the nearest non-forest pixel was calculated to express depth into the forest interior. The two gradients were combined into a single continuous raster in which all values are positive. This metric allows the model to differentiate between forest edge zones, exposed open terrain, and deep forest interior, reflecting the documented wild boar affinity for ecotones between forest cover and agricultural foraging grounds.

#### Terrain Covariates

Slope in degrees and the Terrain Ruggedness Index were derived from the DHM25 using the `terrain()` function of the `terra` package. Because the DHM25 carries no embedded coordinate reference system, the LV03 CRS (EPSG:21781) was assigned manually before processing. The buffered study area bounding box was transformed to LV03 to crop the raw elevation data before computing metrics, optimizing computational efficiency. Both metrics were computed at the native 25-metre resolution of the DHM25 and subsequently reprojected onto the LV95 master grid using bilinear interpolation, which is appropriate for continuous surface variables. Slope quantifies the maximum rate of elevation change across a pixel relative to its eight neighbors, representing the energetic cost of terrain. The Terrain Ruggedness Index quantifies local surface roughness by computing the mean absolute elevation difference between a central pixel and all adjacent cells, identifying sharp topographic transitions and ravines that may function as natural barriers or refugia.

#### Distance to Water

Hydrological features were extracted from the dedicated water layers of swissTLM3D rather than from the general land cover layer `tlm_bb_bodenbedeckung`, which lacks the semantic depth required for accurate hydrological modeling and does not distinguish reliably between above-ground water features and artificially routed or subterranean water.

Standing water bodies were processed from the `tlm_gewaesser_stehendes_gewaesser` layer. The raw geometries are distributed as three-dimensional multi-line strings representing lake shorelines, grouped by a unique water body identifier (`gwl_nr`). To reconstruct these as solid polygon barriers, the three-dimensional Z-coordinates were removed to project all features onto a flat two-dimensional plane, preventing algorithmic failures caused by minor elevation discrepancies along shorelines. The line segments of each water body were then grouped by identifier, unioned, line-merged, and cast to polygons using `st_cast()`. Because islands represent terrestrial habitat within lakes, island polygons were geometrically subtracted from the lake polygons using a Boolean difference operation, producing accurate lake geometries with intact terrestrial islands. Lakes with an area exceeding one square kilometre were separated into a dedicated large-lake mask and treated as absolute barriers in the final burn-in step, assigned `NA` values in the resistance raster. Smaller water bodies were retained as soft barriers with a high but finite resistance.

Flowing water was processed from the `tlm_gewaesser_fliessgewaesser` layer. After removing three-dimensional coordinates, a strict attribute-based filter retained only actual rivers and streams with `objektart == "Fliessgewaesser"` and a surface-level routing attribute (`verlauf`) of "Oberirdisch", "Bruecke", or "Wasserfall". Underground rivers and artificially piped streams were explicitly removed because subterranean water flows do not represent physical barriers or accessible water sources for terrestrial wildlife at the surface.

The processed standing and flowing water geometries were rasterized into a combined binary mask. The Euclidean distance from every pixel to the nearest water feature was then computed to produce the `dist_water` covariate. Initial exploratory models included separate distance variables for standing and flowing water, but this separation introduced variance inflation caused by spatial overlap between the two layers. Unifying them into a single distance-to-water covariate resolved the multicollinearity while retaining the ecologically meaningful signal of proximity to any open water surface.

#### Infrastructure and Barrier Layers

All infrastructure layers were derived from swissTLM3D 2026 in the LV95 reference system. Three feature classes were used: `tlm_strassen_strasse` for the road network, `tlm_oev_eisenbahn` for railways, and `tlm_namen_siedlungsname` for settlement polygons.

Because swissTLM3D stores all linear features as three-dimensional Polyline Z geometries and several downstream operations are incompatible with Z-coordinates, all loaded layers were reduced to two-dimensional geometries immediately after import using `st_zm(drop = TRUE, what = "ZM")`.

A custom preprocessing function, `prep_above_ground()`, was applied to both the road and railway layers to remove all subsurface infrastructure. Wild boar do not perceive roads or railways running through tunnels, underpasses, or inside buildings, and including these features as surface barriers would artificially fragment the resistance raster. The function applied two complementary filters in sequence: a primary numeric filter retaining only features with a `STUFE` value of zero or greater, where negative values indicate first- or second-level underground passages, and a secondary string-based filter removing features with a `KUNSTBAUTE` attribute matching any of the underground structure categories — "Tunnel", "Unterfuehrung", "Unterführung", "in Gebaeude", and "in Gebäude". Both ASCII and Unicode variants were listed because swissTLM3D exports differ across versions. The redundant application of both filters captures edge cases where one attribute is missing or inconsistently coded in particular features.

A second function, `clean_railways()`, was applied exclusively to the railway layer. It removes segments flagged as out of service (`AUSSER_BETRIEB == "Wahr"`) and those identified as funiculars, rack railways, or heritage lines. These specialty rail categories either carry no regular traffic, are restricted to dedicated mountain alignments, or are decommissioned, and treating them as standard fenced barriers would overestimate the barrier effect of railway infrastructure in alpine and peri-alpine areas.

Road features were classified into the three categories described in the data section. For each of the five resulting linear feature classes — fenced roads, main roads, secondary roads, railways, and settlements — a binary presence raster was created using `rasterize()` with `touches = TRUE`, ensuring that pixels intersected by a road or railway centerline received a value of 1 regardless of the fractional coverage. Without this flag, segments of roads thinner than one pixel diagonal can be silently omitted, fragmenting otherwise continuous barriers. A Euclidean distance raster was then computed from each binary mask using `terra::distance()`, producing five continuous covariates: `dist_fenced_road`, `dist_main_road`, `dist_secondary_road`, `dist_settlement`, and `dist_railway`. In addition to these five distance rasters, a combined binary infrastructure mask `r_infra` was constructed aggregating all five feature classes into a single layer, and a separate binary `r_highway` raster was created from the fenced road class alone for use in the final burn-in.

Wildlife crossing structures from `Wildtierpassagen.gdb` were reprojected to LV95, filtered to the buffered cantonal extent, and buffered by 30 metres before rasterization into the binary passage mask `r_passages`. For Canton Zürich, the permanent ASP fences from `Dauerzaeune.shp` were rasterized separately into `r_fences_zh`.

#### Covariate Stack Assembly

Before fitting the iSSF, all independent environmental variables were assembled into a unified covariate stack containing 14 layers: `forest`, `forest_density`, `forest_density_g`, `dist_forest_edge`, `slope`, `tri`, `dist_flowing`, `dist_lakes`, `dist_water`, `dist_fenced_road`, `dist_main_road`, `dist_secondary_road`, `dist_settlement`, and `dist_railway`. All layers were aligned to the 25-metre LV95 master grid by construction, as each had been computed directly on the master grid or reprojected to it before being added to the stack.

### Integrated Step-Selection Function

The iSSF was fitted on in-matrix steps only, comparing each observed transit step against ten random control steps drawn from the empirical step-length and turning-angle distributions of the same dataset. The use of 10 random steps per observed case is consistent with established practice in the iSSF literature and provides sufficient contrast between used and available locations for stable coefficient estimation [@avgar2016].

#### Random Step Generation and Movement Kernel

After filtering the in-matrix steps to remove records with missing step lengths or turning angles and excluding stationary points (step length equal to zero), random control steps were generated using `random_steps()` from the `amt` package. Each random step starts at the same origin as its corresponding observed step and is drawn from a gamma distribution fitted to the observed step-length distribution and a von Mises distribution fitted to the observed turning-angle distribution, ensuring that the available locations reflect the realistic movement capacities of the species. Two movement kernel terms were added to each step record: `log_sl = log(sl_ + 1)` to model the step-length distribution, and `cos_ta = cos(ta_)` to capture directional persistence during transit. Including these terms in the model allows the iSSF to account for the intrinsic movement characteristics of the animal when estimating habitat selection, separating genuine preference from the effects of the movement process itself [@avgar2016].

Because the telemetry CSV contained coordinates in LV03 (EPSG:21781), the native CRS was detected dynamically from the magnitude of the x-coordinates before projecting the step endpoints to the LV95 raster coordinate system for covariate extraction. Covariate values were extracted at the endpoint of each step for both observed and random cases using `terra::extract()`. Steps falling outside the covariate raster extents or returning missing values were excluded from further analysis.

#### Covariate Standardization and Scaling Parameters

All continuous covariates were z-standardized by subtracting the training mean and dividing by the training standard deviation before model fitting, so that the resulting beta coefficients express selection in units of standard deviation and are directly comparable across variables measured on different scales. The mean and standard deviation computed from the Aargau training dataset were saved as a named parameter vector `scale_params`. It was essential to preserve these training statistics because they must be reused unchanged when the model is subsequently projected onto Canton Zürich: applying the Aargau scaling parameters to the Zürich rasters ensures that resistance values in both cantons are expressed on the same behaviorally calibrated scale rather than being normalized independently to their local distributions.

#### Variable Selection

Prior to final model fitting, a systematic variable selection procedure was conducted to address multicollinearity and ensure the parsimony of the covariate set. A standard binary logistic regression was temporarily fitted on the full set of candidate covariates and the Variance Inflation Factor was computed for each predictor using the `car` package. Variables were removed iteratively based on both VIF diagnostics and the statistical significance of their coefficients.

The final retained covariate set consisted of forest density at the 50-metre scale, forest density at the 1000-metre scale, distance to water, distance to main roads, distance to secondary roads, distance to settlements, and distance to railways. VIF values for all retained variables were below 1.4, confirming the absence of critical multicollinearity.

#### Final Model Fitting

The iSSF was fitted using the `clogit()` function from the `survival` package, with a conditional logistic regression stratified by step identifier. Stratification by step identifier ensures that each observed step is compared exclusively against its own 10 random controls, which is the correct inferential structure for a step-selection analysis. The Efron approximation was used to handle tied survival times. The resulting $\hat{\beta}$ coefficients represent log-odds per standard deviation of the corresponding covariate during directed transit movements. A positive coefficient indicates preference for the habitat feature during movement, which translates into lower resistance in the final surface. A negative coefficient indicates avoidance, translating into higher resistance.

### Resistance Surface Construction

The conversion from iSSF coefficients to a resistance raster followed the three-stage procedure of @keeley2016. In the first stage, the linear predictor $\eta$ was computed for every pixel in the Aargau study area by scaling each covariate raster using the saved Aargau training parameters from `scale_params` and then forming the weighted sum:

$$\eta = \sum_k \hat{\beta}_k \cdot x_{k,\text{scaled}}$$

where the sum runs over the seven retained covariates. In the second stage, $\eta$ was normalized to a habitat suitability surface $S \in [0, 1]$ using min-max normalization:

$$S = \frac{\eta - \eta_{\min}}{\eta_{\max} - \eta_{\min}}$$

where $\eta_{\min}$ and $\eta_{\max}$ are the global minimum and maximum of the linear predictor across the entire Aargau study extent. The values $\eta_{\min}$ and $\eta_{\max}$ were saved for reuse during the Zürich transfer. In the third stage, the exponential Keeley transformation was applied to convert suitability into resistance:

$$R = \exp\!\left(C \cdot (1 - S)\right)$$

with the constant $C = 4$ as used by @fischer2024. This yields a resistance surface with a theoretical range of $R_{\min} = \exp(0) = 1$ for the most preferred habitat and $R_{\max} = \exp(4) \approx 54.6$ for the least preferred.

Following the smooth resistance calculation, a deterministic burn-in procedure was applied to assign absolute values to specific landscape features. The order of burn-in assignments is consequential because later assignments overwrite earlier ones where masks overlap. First, small water bodies (those below the one-square-kilometre threshold) were assigned $0.9 \times R_{\max} \approx 49.2$, representing a high but finite barrier cost. Second, all pixels directly occupied by any infrastructure feature in the combined `r_infra` mask — including fenced roads, main roads, secondary roads, railways, and settlement areas — were assigned $R_{\max} \approx 54.6$. Third, pixels in the `r_highway` mask covering fenced motorways and high-speed roads were overwritten with `NA`, designating them as absolute barriers that no connectivity algorithm will route through. Fourth, large lakes exceeding one square kilometre were also assigned `NA`. Finally, wildlife passage pixels were assigned $R_{\min} = 1$, overriding all previous assignments at those locations so that legal crossing structures remain fully permeable regardless of the infrastructure class they traverse. The output resistance raster was masked to the buffered cantonal rectangle and saved as a GeoTIFF alongside a companion habitat suitability raster.

#### Transfer to Canton Zürich

The resistance surface for Canton Zürich was constructed by rebuilding identical covariate layers for the Zürich study extent and applying the Aargau model directly, without any re-estimation of coefficients or re-calibration of scaling parameters. The Zürich covariate rasters were scaled using the Aargau means and standard deviations from `scale_params`, not Zürich's own distributional statistics. The linear predictor $\eta_{\text{ZH}}$ was then normalized using the $\eta_{\min}$ and $\eta_{\max}$ values stored from the Aargau computation rather than from the Zürich-specific $\eta$ distribution:

$$S_{\text{ZH}} = \text{clamp}\!\left(\frac{\eta_{\text{ZH}} - \eta_{\min}}{\eta_{\max} - \eta_{\min}},\ 0,\ 1\right)$$

The `clamp()` function constrains any Zürich suitability values outside the Aargau training range to the interval $[0, 1]$, preventing extrapolation artifacts at the boundaries of the transformed surface. Applying the same scaling parameters and the same $\eta$ normalization range to both cantons ensures that the two resistance surfaces are behaviourally calibrated on the same scale, forming a contiguous surface that can be compared directly and used as a unified input to connectivity analyses spanning both cantons.

The Keeley transformation and burn-in procedure were applied identically to the Zürich surface, with one addition: the permanent ASP fences from the Cantonal Veterinary Office were rasterized into `r_fences_zh` and burned in as absolute barriers (`NA`) immediately after the large-lake burn-in. Wildlife passages were applied last, as in Aargau, overriding the ASP fence burn-in at verified crossing locations. The final Zürich resistance raster was masked to the buffered Zürich rectangle and saved as a GeoTIFF.
